transcript.text: the door on our built in dishwasher just crashes down when you open it now, used to stay put. Hotpoint I think

That's almost always the door balance springs or the cables/cords that connect them to the hinges. There's one on each side of the dishwasher, and they're what hold the door steady. When one snaps or comes unhooked, the door drops. If it's completely free-falling, often both have gone, or the cord on one side has frayed through.

## Check it yourself

1. Turn off the power at the isolator switch or plug.
2. Remove the plinth/kickboard at the bottom (usually clips off or has a couple of screws).
3. Look at the lower sides of the machine with a torch. You should see a spring on each side, attached to a cord or cable that runs to the door hinge.

You'll typically find one of these:
• A snapped spring
• A broken or frayed cord/cable (these wear out more often than the springs)
• A spring that's just popped off its hook. You can sometimes simply re-hook it.

On some built-in models, you need to unscrew the dishwasher from the worktop and slide it forward a few inches to get proper access. Disconnecting the water isn't usually necessary if you're careful not to stretch the hoses.

## Getting parts

• Find the model number on a sticker on the edge of the door or inner side of the tub when the door is open.
• Search "Hotpoint [model number] door spring kit". Kits with springs and cords are cheap (often £10–20) from places like eSpares, Partmaster, or Amazon.
• Replace both sides at once, even if only one broke. The other is usually worn too, and uneven tension can twist the door.

## Worth knowing

• Integrated (fully built-in) models: if a kitchen fitter added a heavy wooden door panel, the springs may have been under strain from day one. Some models have adjustable tension, so check the manual.
• If the springs and cords look fine, the hinge itself may be broken or bent, which is a slightly bigger job.

## Meanwhile

Open the door slowly by hand. A falling door can damage the hinges, chip the tub, or hurt someone's foot. Be especially careful if you have kids around.

It's a very doable DIY job, usually 30–60 minutes. If you can tell me the model number, I can help you find the right part.

Thanks. The model number sticker on the door edge is partly peeled, but I can see it starts with LTF. I had a look under the plinth with a torch and there's a loose spring hanging down on the right side. I can't slide the machine out though, it's screwed to the worktop and I'm not confident doing that.

A loose spring on the right side is good news. It's the most likely cause, and it may just need re-hooking.

## First, see what's actually broken

With the power off, shine the torch on the loose spring:

• Spring intact, hook end free: It's just come unhooked. You may be able to reattach it without moving the machine.
• Spring snapped: You'll see a broken coil or a missing hook end. It needs replacing.
• Spring fine but the cord is broken or frayed: It's the cord, not the spring. This is very common on Hotpoints.

Also check the left side. If the door is crashing right down, the left spring may be stretched or worn too.

## Trying to re-hook it without moving the machine

If it's just unhooked:

1. Find where it should attach. There's usually a slot or hook on the base frame, or the end of the cord coming down from the door hinge.
2. With the door closed (that's when the tension is lowest), use long-nose pliers to stretch the spring and hook it back on.
3. Open and close the door gently to test.

It can be fiddly in a tight space. If you can't reach comfortably, don't force it.

## About sliding it out

It's usually less daunting than it looks. There are normally just two screws through small brackets at the top of the door opening, going up into the underside of the worktop. You undo those, wind the front feet up a little, and ease it forward a few inches. But if you'd rather not, that's completely reasonable.

## Finding the full model number

"LTF" fits Hotpoint's integrated range, but you'll need the full number to get the right parts. Try:

• The other side edge of the door, or the inside rim of the tub
• The manual, receipt, or kitchen fitter's paperwork
• Your Hotpoint registration email, if you registered it
• The photo on the peeled sticker. Sometimes a phone photo with the flash on picks up faded print.

## If you'd rather not do it yourself

A local appliance repair person will do this quickly, often in under an hour. Expect to pay roughly £60–100 including parts, depending on your area. Hotpoint's own engineers also do it but usually cost more. Tell them "loose door spring, right side, LTF model" when you book so they bring the right kit.
The left side still has a bit of tension, but the right has none at all. I can see the spring hanging loose on the right, but I can't tell from down there whether it's snapped or just unhooked.

Here are a few ways to tell from where you are.

## Get a better look

• Use your phone camera. Hold it down low with the flash or torch on and take a photo or video, or zoom in. It's much easier than craning your neck, and you can enlarge the image.
• Compare it with the left side. Look at how the left spring attaches at each end. That shows you what the right one should look like and where it should hook on.

## What to look for on the loose spring

Check both ends:

• Both ends have a neat, complete curled hook: It's just come unhooked. You may be able to re-hook it.
• One end is a sharp, straight bit of wire, or the hook is missing: It's snapped. The missing piece may be lying on the floor under the machine.
• The spring looks fine but is attached to a cord or cable that's broken or frayed: The cord has gone, not the spring.

## Feel it (power off)

If you can reach it, gently run your fingers along it, carefully, as a snapped end can be sharp. A broken hook is easy to feel even when you can't see it.

## Check the length

If you can pull it out far enough, compare its length with the left one. A snapped spring is usually noticeably shorter or missing its end loop.

## Either way

Since the left still has some tension but isn't holding the door properly, it's probably worn too. Even if the right one only came unhooked, it's worth ordering a pair (springs and cords) once you've got the full model number, so both sides are balanced.

Let me know what you see and I'll help with the next step.
I tried the phone camera idea but it's hard to tell from that angle. Is there anything else I can do to check without sliding it out?

Yes, there are a few more things to try. Honestly, though, you may not need to know for sure (see the end).

## 1. Watch it while someone opens the door

This is the most useful test. With the power off, lie down with the torch and have someone slowly open and close the door.

• The spring moves as the door opens: The cord and top attachment are fine. The problem is at the bottom end, where it's either unhooked or snapped at the base hook.
• The spring doesn't move at all: The cord has broken or come off the hinge, so the spring is just dangling.

## 2. Feel the ends with gloves on

Wear gloves (a snapped end can be sharp) and reach in to feel the free end of the spring. A proper hook feels like a smooth curled loop. A snapped one feels like a straight, sharp bit of wire or an open, broken coil.

## 3. Look for the missing piece

Shine the torch along the floor under the machine and behind the plinth area. If you find a small curled bit of wire, the spring has snapped.

## 4. Use a cheap inspection camera

If you want a proper look, a USB or Wi-Fi endoscope camera costs about £10–20 online. It plugs into your phone, and the small camera on a flexible cable can get right in beside the spring. It's handy to have for other jobs too.

## Why it might not matter much

Whichever it turns out to be, the sensible fix is the same: a new spring and cord kit for both sides, since the left one is clearly worn too. So the diagnosis mainly tells you whether you can get the door working temporarily by re-hooking it.

Fitting new springs and cords on most built-in Hotpoints does usually mean easing the machine forward. If you're not comfortable with that, it's a quick, cheap job for an appliance repair person. Giving them the full model number when you book means they can bring the right kit.
